tldr-heading.old_plain: What foreigners must know about the autónomo route in Spain
tldr-heading.new_plain: Becoming self-employed in Spain: key points

tldr-b2.old_plain: • Applicants need a NIE, Spanish tax residence, and a Spanish bank account before any registration can proceed.
tldr-b2.new_plain: • Applicants need a NIE and a Spanish bank account before registration, and non-EU nationals also need a residence permit that allows self-employment.

tldr-b3.old_plain: • Registration involves two separate filings: Modelo 036 or 037 with the AEAT and Modelo TA0521 with Seguridad Social.
tldr-b3.new_plain:
• Registration involves two separate filings: the census registration with the AEAT on Modelo 036 (Modelo 037 was abolished on 3 February 2025) and the alta in the RETA with Seguridad Social, which self-employed workers must complete electronically.
  • For 2026, autónomo contributions follow 15 net-income brackets, from €205.88 a month at the lowest minimum base to €607.35 a month at the minimum base of the top bracket.

tldr-b4.old_plain: • New autónomos benefit from the tarifa plana of €87 per month for the first 12 months, extendable in some cases to 24 months.
tldr-b4.new_plain: • The tarifa plana reduces contributions for the first 12 months and can extend to 24 months if net income stays below the annual SMI, but the €80 amount is confirmed only for 2023 to 2025 and the 2026 amount needs checking.

tldr-b6.old_plain: • Working with a specialist lawyer avoids the most common documentary errors during the first year of activity.
tldr-b6.new_plain: • Services invoiced to a business client in the UK or the US are generally not subject to Spanish VAT, while a business client in another EU country accounts for the VAT itself under the reverse-charge rule.

intro1.old_plain: Spain offers one of the most accessible self-employment regimes in the European Union, and international entrepreneurs increasingly choose it as their base.
intro1.new_plain: Spain lets foreign professionals work for their own account under the autónomo regime.

intro2.old_plain: Becoming self-employed in Spain gives professionals immediate access to a market of 47 million residents, favourable tax incentives in the first years of activity and full Schengen mobility.
intro2.new_plain: Becoming self-employed in Spain gives professionals access to the Spanish market and to a reduced contribution during the first months of activity.

prereq-residence.old_plain: • Tax residence in Spain: applicants must spend more than 183 days per year in Spain or have their main economic activity centred here.
prereq-residence.new_plain: • Tax residence in Spain: under article 9 of the personal income tax law you are tax resident in Spain when you spend more than 183 days in a calendar year in Spain or when the main base of your activities or economic interests is here.

census-forms.old_plain:
Two forms cover the census filing:

  • Modelo 036: the full form used for complex or higher-turnover activities.
  • Modelo 037: the simplified version, suitable for most freelancers.

The choice depends on the activity type and the applicable VAT regime, and the correct economic activity code is selected from the official IAE Epigraphs list.
census-forms.new_plain:
The census filing uses Modelo 036. The AEAT abolished the simplified Modelo 037 through Orden HAC/1526/2024, in force since 3 February 2025, so freelancers now use Modelo 036 as well.

The correct economic activity code is selected from the official IAE Epigraphs list, and it affects the VAT regime that applies to you.

roi.new_plain: must also register in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI) and obtain a VIES number, as detailed in our note on

alta.old_plain: Applicants book an appointment online at their local office and complete Modelo TA0521, the specific form for autónomo registration.
alta.new_plain: Self-employed workers must handle registration, contributions and notifications with Seguridad Social electronically, a duty in force since 1 October 2018. The alta is requested in the Seguridad Social electronic office with a digital certificate, an electronic DNI or Cl@ve.

alta-free.old_plain: The process is free of charge and typically takes 24 to 48 hours.

contributions.old_plain:
Since 2023, autónomo contributions follow a progressive net-income model with 15 income brackets.

New autónomos benefit from the tarifa plana of €87 per month for the first 12 months, extendable to 24 months where net income remains below the SMI.

After the reduced period, contributions align with actual net earnings and typically range from €220 to €610 per month.
contributions.new_plain:
Since 2023, autónomo contributions follow a progressive net-income model with 15 income brackets, three in the reduced table and twelve in the general table.

For 2026, Real Decreto-ley 3/2026 (article 3.4) keeps the 2025 tables in force until a new budget law replaces them, and Orden PJC/297/2026 sets the 2026 bases and rates. The combined rate is 31.50%: 28.30% for common contingencies, 1.30% for professional contingencies, 0.90% for cessation of activity, 0.10% for vocational training and 0.90% for the intergenerational equity mechanism.

BracketMonthly net incomeMinimum baseMonthly contribution at the minimum base
Reduced table, bracket 1Up to €670€653.59€205.88
General table, bracket 12Above €6,000€1,928.10€607.35

You can choose a higher base within the limits of your bracket, and the full tables with the minimum and maximum base of each bracket are in the Orden.

The tarifa plana is a reduced contribution for people who register for the first time or who were not registered in the previous two years. Article 38 ter of the Self-Employed Workers’ Statute (Ley 20/2007) provides a reduced quota for the first 12 complete calendar months and, if net income stays below the annual SMI, for a further 12 months. The amount is set by the budget law, and the BOE text records €80 a month for 2023 to 2025 only.

The 2026 amount is therefore not confirmed as at 6 October 2026. Contact us before your alta to confirm the amount that applies to your start date.

records-1.old_plain: keep accounting records for at least four years and observe every filing deadline
records-1.new_plain: keep their accounting records and observe every filing deadline

records-2.new_plain:
Spanish tax deadlines.

On retention, the tax authority’s right to assess a tax year expires after four years under article 66 of the General Tax Law, while article 30 of the Commercial Code requires businesses to keep their books and supporting documents for six years from the last entry. Ask us which period applies to your activity.

mistake-penalty.old_plain: • Missing the quarterly Modelo 303 or 130 deadlines, with penalties starting at €100 per return.
mistake-penalty.new_plain: • Missing the quarterly Modelo 303 or 130 deadlines: a return filed late without a prior request from the tax office carries a surcharge of 1% plus 1% for each complete month of delay, rising to 15% after 12 months (article 27 of the General Tax Law).

us-uk-section.old_plain: Common mistakes when becoming self-employed in Spain
us-uk-section.new_plain:
Becoming self-employed in Spain with US or UK clients

This section covers Spanish rules only. Coordinate your US or UK tax filings and any home-country social security position with your home-country adviser.

Invoicing clients outside Spain: VAT

Article 69 of the Spanish VAT law treats a service to a business customer as supplied in Spain when the customer’s business is established in Spain, subject to the special rules in articles 70 and 72. A service invoiced to a business client in the UK or the US is therefore generally outside Spanish VAT, so Spanish VAT is not charged on that invoice.

For a business client in another EU country, the client is the taxable person and accounts for the VAT itself, under the reverse-charge mechanism. Article 6.1.m of the invoicing regulation (Real Decreto 1619/2012) requires the invoice to carry the words «inversión del sujeto pasivo» when the customer is the taxable person. The AEAT guidance on identification for operations with other EU businesses explains the ROI registration and the Modelo 349 statement.

The ROI and Modelo 349 relate to operations with other EU Member States, and the UK has not been a Member State since Brexit. Private customers outside the EU follow a different rule: article 69 lists services such as advertising, consultancy, legal and accounting services, data processing and translation as not supplied in Spain when the recipient is not a business and is established outside the EU. Other services to consumers need a case-by-case check, so contact us before you invoice consumers abroad.

Contributions and the tarifa plana

The 2026 contribution tables and the position on the tarifa plana are set out in the section on autónomo contributions above. The 2026 amount of the reduced contribution is not confirmed, so ask us before you plan your first-year cash flow.

Social security coordination with the US and the UK

The US-Spain social security agreement, known as a totalisation agreement and in force since 1 April 1988, covers social security contributions and benefits, not income tax. Article 4 provides:

A person who would otherwise be covered under the laws of both Contracting States with respect to self-employment shall be subject to the laws of only the Contracting State of which he is a resident.

The US Social Security Administration summary adds that a worker who is normally self-employed in one country and transfers the business to the other for five years or fewer stays covered in the country of origin. It also says that Spanish periods count towards a US benefit only if you have at least six US credits, and that US periods count towards a Spanish benefit only if you have at least one year of coverage in the Spanish system.

For British freelancers, article SSC.10(3)(a) of the Protocol on Social Security Coordination in the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement provides:

a person pursuing an activity as an employed or self-employed person in a State shall be subject to the legislation of that State;

Article SSC.7 of the same Protocol requires a State, to the extent necessary, to take into account periods of insurance, employment, self-employment or residence completed in another State when its own rules make a benefit conditional on completing periods. People who were already in a cross-border situation between the UK and an EU Member State at the end of the transition period can remain covered under article 30 of the Withdrawal Agreement for as long as that situation continues without interruption.

Whether your US or UK periods count towards a future pension, and whether you need a certificate of coverage, depends on your history and dates. Contact Félix Delaguía at felix.delaguia@delaguialuzon.com or on +34 963 74 16 57 to confirm your case.

Tax residence and Modelo 720

Registering as an autónomo and working from Spain usually brings you within the Spanish tax residence tests described above, and a tax resident is taxed in Spain on worldwide income. Our guide to UK Spain double taxation explains the 183-day rule and residence certificates.

Tax residents who hold accounts, securities or property abroad must also report them on the Modelo 720 once a category exceeds €50,000, between 1 January and 31 March of the following year, under the general tax procedures regulation, and the AEAT filing page gives the dates for each campaign. Read our guide to the Modelo 720 before your first return, and our note on social security for cross-border teleworkers if you also work remotely for a foreign employer.
